summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework. State-level protections specific to this jurisdiction have narrowed: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003, which barred discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation, was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010, which also covered gender identity and sexual orientation, lost two of its operative provisions when the Supreme Federal Court declared Articles 2 VI and VII unconstitutional in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018. The state constitution's anti-discrimination clause, in force since 2002, lists sexual orientation but does not address discrimination against transgender people.

What remains of Complementary Law No. 527 is the jurisdiction's principal conduct rule for visitors. It penalises private legal entities and, where applicable, state public servants that promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation. The acts it defines include violent, coercive, intimidating or vexatious conduct; barring entry to or stay in places of free public access; service differentiated in ways the law does not require; refusing, preferring against or surcharging hotel, motel and pension lodging and the rental, purchase, acquisition or lease of movable and immovable property; and prohibiting expressions of affection that are permitted to others. Penalties are R$2,500, rising to R$5,000 on repeat, with 30-day suspension of an annual licence or revocation of monthly, daily or seasonal licences and a 30-day bar on renewal; complaints go to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defence of the Citizen, fines are directed to the State Civil Police Improvement Fund, and state servants face suspension of up to 30 days.

Marriage formalities are processed locally without a sex restriction. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorised notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses and without observance of any gender limitation, extending Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable unions recognised since 2011; couples where both partners reside in the state could then formalise civil marriage at registry level. In Florianópolis, Judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived more than ten years in a stable relationship with a Brazilian partner.

Documents recording a non-binary gender have been issued in Santa Catarina since 2020 through the courts and notarial offices, though no state law provides for them. In 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in the state to change documents judicially to reflect a neutral gender. A judicial action remains necessary in the absence of a state recognition law, and legal sex is still recorded on birth certificates.

Access to sex-segregated facilities is contested in the state. Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 on 21 January 2026, requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms. From 18 June 2026 the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signage indicating that restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity, in direct tension with the state requirement.

The leading public-accommodation case began in a Florianópolis shopping mall in 2014, when a trans woman was stopped by mall security from using the women's restroom. A lower court awarded 15,000 reais in compensation for pain and suffering under the Consumer Defence Code, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned the award, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court voted 8-3 to dismiss her appeal on the procedural ground that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions. The court withdrew the general repercussion it had recognised, so no binding constitutional ruling on trans restroom access was issued. In August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was taken to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Florianópolis is among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, although the legal rights are the same.
tangentialFactors:
The state legislature has been the site of sustained anti-LGBTQIA+ activity. Between January 2019 and June 2025 state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills; the proposals included a ban on neutral language in official government communications and a bar on minors receiving hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care. Four of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none was enacted. As of 2025, 11 of the 19 had been authored by the Liberal Party. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, which remained under review as of 18 August 2026.

A 2026 tally counted at least 271 unconstitutional laws, bills and normative acts advanced by the Legislative Assembly and its 295 municipal chambers between January 2015 and October 2025, all of a type already declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. Forty-one per cent attacked gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, and about 70 per cent of that share involved the trans and travesti community; 36 per cent were already in force, only 11 per cent had been judicially annulled, the measures were concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí, and the pace accelerated over the five years to 2025.

State courts have enforced protection against anti-LGBT conduct in the family. On 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina ordered the parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay 100,000 reais in compensation after they expelled him from the home and exposed his sexual orientation on social media.
localsOnly:
Rules governing schools and public language have moved against transgender residents and then been reversed in court. Gender-neutral language was banned in state schools by a decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 until the Supreme Federal Court overturned it on 6 May 2025, and a Joinville law of 20 December 2021 banning neutral language in public office was struck down by the Court of Justice on 3 August 2022. A 2015 Tubarão law prohibiting the teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools was struck down by the Supreme Federal Court on 15 October 2025. On 1 April 2026, in a law published 6 April, Governor Jorginho Mello allowed parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics.

For residents liable to military service, the Army treats any person in the draft cohort who expresses a gender identity other than male and who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or a civil-registry amendment as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals, and considers them exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting the requirements of the Federal Constitution, the Military Service Law, its implementing regulations and the 2024 General Conscription Plan.
outOfScopeNotes:
The reported volume of anti-trans violence in Santa Catarina is not established by the available sources in a way that permits comparison with the state's general homicide rate. A count of three murders of trans people recorded in the state in 2024 and a 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook figure of 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals are raw counts without a population denominator, and the yearbook attributes the low recorded rates to underreporting, which makes the true incidence unknowable from these figures.

The December 2023 Legislative Assembly bill barring transgender women from women's sports was still under review as of 18 August 2026; its outcome is unresolved.

The 2018 partial annulment of Complementary Law No. 527 removed two of its enumerated discriminatory acts, and the scope of what the surviving provisions cover in practice is not documented in the available sources.
